section_summary: This section follows Japan’s financial position from January through April 1937, focusing on exchange controls, the yen, government borrowing, trade, and gold shipments. Embassy telegrams and paraphrases are interspersed with Treasury correspondence, records of meetings with Japanese officials, internal assessments, and filing notes. The section ends with the opening of a longer State Department study of Japan’s capacity to finance military spending.

subfiles.title: Embassy assessment of Japan’s financial situation, conclusion
subfiles.about: Assesses pressure on the yen and government bonds after the 1937–38 budget proposal.
subfiles.summary: Grew links the January 8 exchange controls to yen weakness, speculative imports, and scarce stabilization funds. He expects rising debt and prices but considers an imminent financial collapse unlikely.

subfiles.title: Compliments to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.about: Conveys the Treasury Secretary’s and State Department’s compliments on Grew’s January 13 report.
subfiles.summary: Compliments Grew on telegram No. 5.

subfiles.title: Moore’s reply concerning compliments to Grew
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the suggestion to compliment Grew.
subfiles.summary: Moore says he has sent the requested cable.

subfiles.title: Request for further financial reports
subfiles.about: Requests reports on further Japanese financial developments.
subfiles.summary: Asks Grew to report further developments when possible.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Grew’s January 13 telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards five paraphrased copies of Grew’s telegram No. 5.
subfiles.summary: Encloses five copies of the paraphrase.

subfiles.title: Treasury request to compliment Grew
subfiles.about: Asks Moore to cable Grew with compliments on telegram No. 5.
subfiles.summary: Requests a congratulatory cable to Grew.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 9 on exchange controls
subfiles.about: Reports early effects of exchange controls and concern over deficit bonds.
subfiles.summary: Import exchange remains unsettled despite resumed interbank payments. The yen holds at 1s 2d, prices rise, and rumors suggest Governor Fukai may resign over deficit bonds.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 9
subfiles.about: Restates the Embassy’s report on exchange delays, prices, and bond financing.
subfiles.summary: Banks seek import histories before settling bills; a later rush could pressure the yen. Rising prices and possible disagreement between Fukai and Baba remain concerns.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of January 16 and 18 telegrams
subfiles.about: Forwards five copies each of two paraphrased telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Encloses telegrams No. 7 and No. 9.

subfiles.title: Treasury response to Embassy report
subfiles.about: Responds to Grew’s January 18 financial telegram.
subfiles.summary: Brief reply to telegram No. 9; OCR obscures its substance.

subfiles.title: Inquiry on exchange permits and clearance
subfiles.about: Asks about permits and whether exchange transactions are clearing.
subfiles.summary: Requests details on permit issuance and exchange clearance.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 10 on blocked American payments
subfiles.about: Examines whether exchange controls block money owed to Americans.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy cannot estimate affected orders but believes little money actually due to Americans is blocked. Officials promise permits for legitimate prior contracts and continued support for the yen.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 10
subfiles.about: Restates assurances concerning American payments and exchange permits.
subfiles.summary: Existing credits continue to be negotiated, and Japanese officials expect to approve legitimate imports once administrative difficulties ease.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of exchange-control telegrams
subfiles.about: Forwards Tokyo, London, and Paris telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Encloses four telegrams, including Tokyo’s exchange-control reply.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 17 on the political crisis
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Reports market reactions to the Hirota Cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: The yen and bonds remain firm; industrial shares fall on fears of stronger military control.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 17
subfiles.about: Restates the market effects of the Japanese political crisis.
subfiles.summary: Exchange controls steady the yen while industrial stocks react to cabinet uncertainty.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of telegram No. 17
subfiles.about: Forwards a paraphrase of Grew’s political-crisis telegram.
subfiles.summary: Encloses five copies of telegram No. 17.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Katsuo Okazaki
subfiles.about: Records Japanese concern over U.S. press accounts of exchange control.
subfiles.summary: Okazaki tells Dooman that press reports wrongly imply secrecy, obstruction of American business, and impending yen devaluation. He requests clarification after a Japanese financial official explains the ordinance.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Ukawa, Okazaki, and Taylor
subfiles.about: Records a Treasury meeting on Japan’s exchange-control ordinance and its public explanation.
subfiles.summary: Ukawa explains the January 8 ordinance as a temporary response to speculative imports and insists Japan will maintain the yen at 1s 2d. Okazaki cites military spending, Australian trade, and tariff speculation, while allowing that controls could continue or tighten after July. Taylor acknowledges bankers’ concerns about delays, and the participants discuss a short public statement.

subfiles.title: Summary of the January 8 finance ordinance
subfiles.about: Summarizes permit requirements and exceptions for foreign exchange and import credits.
subfiles.summary: The temporary ordinance requires permits for most exchange transactions and import letters of credit, with specified value and preexisting-shipment exceptions. It also regulates use of foreign currency assets and bank payments ordered from abroad.

subfiles.title: Draft press release on Ukawa’s Treasury visit
subfiles.about: Drafts a notice that Ukawa explained Japan’s exchange controls to Treasury officials.
subfiles.summary: Draft announces Ukawa’s Treasury visit and its purpose.

subfiles.title: Transmittal concerning Treasury discussion
subfiles.about: Forwards material on the discussion of exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: Partly illegible transmittal refers to discussion by a Treasury official.

subfiles.title: Press release on Ukawa’s Treasury visit
subfiles.about: Announces Ukawa’s explanation of Japanese exchange-control measures.
subfiles.summary: States that Ukawa briefed a Treasury officer on the January 8 controls.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to February 2 telegram
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram on reaction to Japan’s new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Notes favorable reaction and confidence in Yuki as Finance Minister.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 48 on exchange permits
subfiles.about: Reports the pace of permits and prospective import quantities.
subfiles.summary: Permits gradually cover earlier contracts, especially U.S. cotton, but none for new business are confirmed. The exchange market is firmer, and announced raw-material quantities appear to be planning benchmarks.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 48
subfiles.about: Restates the Embassy’s report on permits and raw-material imports.
subfiles.summary: Cotton receives priority for permits; other importers face delays. Banks settle approved contracts normally, and import quantities likely guide exchange planning.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of February exchange telegrams
subfiles.about: Forwards paraphrases of telegrams No. 24 and No. 48.
subfiles.summary: Encloses five copies of each telegram.

subfiles.title: Assessment of Japan’s economic and financial outlook
subfiles.about: Compares pessimistic press analysis with official assessments of Japan’s economy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds Japan’s debt, trade balance, and slowing export growth manageable on economic grounds. It identifies military policy, spending, and state reorganization as the decisive uncertainties. Its author sees no immediate danger of a major catastrophe but acknowledges a narrow margin of safety.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 59 on Yuki’s financial policies
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Reports improved confidence, a smaller budget, and firmer exchange.
subfiles.summary: Grew attributes a brighter outlook to Yuki’s policies, a reduced budget, and effective exchange controls. He discusses deficit-bond sales, possible specie shipments, and repurchase of Japanese dollar bonds.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 59
subfiles.about: Restates the improved outlook under Yuki.
subfiles.summary: Confidence rises as prices slow and the yen holds at 1s 2d. Some observers expect limited gold exports or dollar-bond purchases.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 64 on rumored gold shipments
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Checks press reports of Japanese gold exports.
subfiles.summary: Tsushima calls reported shipment amounts fabricated and says no schedule is fixed, though future shipments to the United States are contemplated.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 64
subfiles.about: Restates Tsushima’s denial of specific gold-shipment plans.
subfiles.summary: Tsushima says reserves remain ample and asks whether small U.S.-bound shipments would trouble the Treasury.

subfiles.title: Treasury request to continue reports
subfiles.about: Confirms that Treasury wants continuing financial telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Treasury finds Grew’s reports valuable and requests their continuation.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Embassy telegram No. 64
subfiles.about: Repeats the report denying fixed gold-shipment plans.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate copy of the February 27 gold-shipment telegram.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 67 on planned gold shipment
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed shipment of Bank of Japan gold to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Tsushima says approximately 13,900 kilograms may leave Kobe March 9 for San Francisco.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Embassy telegram No. 67
subfiles.about: Restates the proposed March gold shipment and expected use of proceeds.
subfiles.summary: Gold proceeds reportedly would support the yen through Yokohama Specie Bank’s New York office.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of telegram No. 67
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s gold-shipment telegram.
subfiles.summary: Encloses five paraphrased copies of telegram No. 67.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to February 15 despatch
subfiles.about: Points to Grew’s despatch on Japanese finances and new-cabinet policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch No. 2257.

subfiles.title: Government finance and January economic conditions
subfiles.about: Reviews January’s budget, trade, prices, and financial markets.
subfiles.summary: The report describes an unfavorable but manageable fiscal position, with deficit bonds and military spending central concerns. January imports exceeded exports sharply, commodity prices rose, and exchange controls supported the yen.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 114 on renewed gold shipments
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s decision to resume gold shipments to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Tsushima confidentially reports planned shipments totaling 15,000 kilograms, beginning April 21.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of telegram No. 114
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s report on renewed gold shipments.
subfiles.summary: Encloses five paraphrased copies of telegram No. 114.

subfiles.title: Embassy telegram No. 116 on Yuki’s bankers’ address
subfiles.about: Reports Yuki’s appeal for banks to support government economic plans.
subfiles.summary: Yuki urges planned investment, selective import restrictions, Manchurian finance, and participation in an international conference.

subfiles.title: Hull’s letter to the President on Japan’s finances
subfiles.about: Sends revised conclusions on Japan’s financial and economic capacity.
subfiles.summary: Hull transmits the updated study’s summary and conclusions.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about missing annual-report copies
subfiles.about: Seeks two missing copies of Japan’s 1936 financial annual.
subfiles.summary: Asks whether copies were detached or forwarded elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Handwritten routing note on annual-report copies
subfiles.about: Directs a check for detached copies.
subfiles.summary: Asks staff to look for copies in the records section.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about unreceived despatch enclosures
subfiles.about: Seeks information about enclosures missing from the attached despatch.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Far Eastern Affairs has not received the enclosures.

subfiles.title: Notice of annual-report copies sent with despatch
subfiles.about: Traces two copies of the 1936 Financial and Economic Annual of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Says two copies left Publications with despatch No. 2353 but have not returned.

subfiles.title: Request for despatch enclosures
subfiles.about: Requests the annual-report enclosures to Tokyo despatch No. 2353.
subfiles.summary: Requests copies of Japan’s 1936 financial annual.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2353 transmitting Japan’s financial annual
subfiles.about: Transmits three copies of Japan’s 1936 Financial and Economic Annual.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards three copies received from the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Japan’s financial and economic situation
subfiles.about: Updates a 1934 study of Japan’s ability to finance armaments and military activity.
subfiles.summary: The opening pages review rising government spending, revenue shortfalls, bond issues, and debt since 1933. The authors judge the debt large but not yet dangerously so and identify banks’ capacity to absorb bonds as essential to continued military finance. The memorandum continues beyond page 80.
